props.title: Baby It's You
props.initialSlug: High school romance tests class divide in 1960s NJ

sections.content: Baby It's You (1983) represents John Sayles' most polished exploration of class dynamics in 1960s America, following the unlikely romance between Jewish honor student Jill Rosen (Rosanna Arquette) and working-class Italian "Sheik" (Vincent Spano). The film captures the cultural upheaval of 1967 through precise period details and a killer soundtrack featuring Bruce Springsteen tracks (before they became prohibitively expensive for films). Like American Graffiti (1973) and Diner (1982), it uses coming-of-age drama to examine a specific moment of societal transition. movies.title: The Last Picture Show
movies.slug: Peter Bogdanovich's stark portrayal of small-town Texas teens facing adulthood and disillusionment

sections.content: Sayles brings his independent sensibilities to what could have been a conventional teen romance, refusing to sand down the rough edges of class conflict and cultural identity. The film shares DNA with Valley Girl (1983) in its examination of cross-cultural teenage romance, but takes a grittier, more realistic approach. The progression from high school to college life mirrors similar territory covered in Breaking Away (1979), though with sharper political undertones reflecting the Vietnam era's social upheaval. SUBHEAD: Class and Cultural Identity in 1960s Teen Films

The film's strength lies in how it subverts expectations of both teen and period films. Unlike Grease (1978) or American Graffiti (1973), it doesn't romanticize its era. Instead, it shows characters struggling with real limitations of class and background. Jill's journey to Sarah Lawrence and Sheik's attempt to break into show business in Miami highlight how social mobility remained constrained even during the supposedly freewheeling '60s. The film's use of Bruce Springsteen music (including "It's Hard to Be a Saint in the City" and "She's the One") reinforces its working-class authenticity.
